```{r}
#| warning: false
# Load packages
library(survival)
```

These are the results of a Cox regression:

```{r}
#| warning: false
# Load data
d <- gbsg

# # Values of variable
# range(d$rfstime)
# range(d$nodes)

# Change survival time to years
d$rfstime <- d$rfstime / 365.25

# Cox regression with interaction
mod_01 <- coxph(formula = Surv(time = rfstime,
                               event = status) ~ meno * nodes,
                data = d)
summary(mod_01)

# # Schoenfeld residual test
# cox.zph(mod_01)
```


The data come from a 1984-1989 study of German patients with node-positive breast cancer.
The variables are as follows:

- `rfstime` is "recurrence free survival time",
i.e., the number of years to recurrence, death, or last follow-up.
- `status` is 1 for recurrence or death and 0
for alive without recurrence.
- `meno` is 1 for postmenopausal patients
and 0 for premenopausal patients.
- `nodes` is the number of positive lymph nodes.
Values range from 1 to 51.

Please answer the following questions.

## Problem 1

For each of the following,
please write a number or mathematical expression representing the statement.
Since I'm not letting you use calculators, you don't have to do any computation.
For example, for the statement, "The number of toes on a typical human being,"
you could write "10" or "5 + 5".
If it's impossible to write a number or mathematical expression representing the statement
because not enough information has been provided,
please write, "Impossible."
Each is worth one point.


### Part (a)

The hazard ratio at time $t$ comparing postmenopausal to premenopausal patients,
among patients who have no positive lymph nodes.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}


1.082660

$$
\begin{align*}
    \frac{\lambda_j(t)}{\lambda_i(t)} &= \frac{\lambda_0(t) \exp\left(0.079421 \texttt{meno}_j + 0.060853 \texttt{nodes}_j - 0.003607 \texttt{meno}_j\times\texttt{nodes}_j\right)}{\lambda_0(t) \exp\left(0.079421 \texttt{meno}_i + 0.060853 \texttt{nodes}_i - 0.003607 \texttt{meno}_i\times\texttt{nodes}_i\right)} \\
    &= \frac{ \exp\left(0.079421 (1) + 0.060853 (0) - 0.003607 (1)\times(0)\right)}{ \exp\left(0.079421 (0) + 0.060853 (0) - 0.003607 (0)\times(0)\right)} \\
    &= \exp\left(0.079421 \right) \\
    &= 1.082660
\end{align*}
$$
You might have thought to yourself, "These patients have 'node-positive' breast cancer,
and the minimum number of positive lymph nodes is 1.
How can we estimate a hazard ratio among patients who have no positive lymph nodes?"
The interpretation of the coefficient is the same,
even though there aren't any observed patients with no positive lymph nodes.
We are extrapolating beyond our observed data,
which is never a good idea.
But, that's how you interpret this coefficient.

:::
        
### Part (b)

The hazard rate at time $t$ for a postmenopausal patient
with one positive lymph node.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

Impossible.

Cox regression returns hazard ratios, not hazard rates.

A couple people wrote $h_0(t) \exp(0.079421 + 0.060853 - 0.003607)$
in response to this question.
If you would admit this as a correct answer,
you should admit any function of $t$.
If a student wrote, for example, $h_0(t) \exp(5)$,
they could argue that
$$
h_0(t) = g_0(t) \exp(0.079421 + 0.060853 - 0.003607 - 5) \text{,}
$$
so that
$$
\begin{align*}
    h_0(t) \exp(5) &=  g_0(t) \exp(0.079421 + 0.060853 - 0.003607 - 5) \exp(5) \\
    &=  g_0(t) \exp(0.079421 + 0.060853 - 0.003607) \text{.} 
\end{align*}
$$
The point here is that Cox regression does not estimate hazard rates.

:::

### Part (c)

The hazard ratio at time $t$ comparing patients with one positive lymph node
to patients with zero positive lymph nodes, 
among patients who are premenopausal.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

1.062743

$$
\begin{align*}
    \frac{\lambda_j(t)}{\lambda_i(t)} &= \frac{\lambda_0(t) \exp\left(0.079421 \texttt{meno}_j + 0.060853 \texttt{nodes}_j - 0.003607 \texttt{meno}_j\times\texttt{nodes}_j\right)}{\lambda_0(t) \exp\left(0.079421 \texttt{meno}_i + 0.060853 \texttt{nodes}_i - 0.003607 \texttt{meno}_i\times\texttt{nodes}_i\right)} \\
    &= \frac{ \exp\left(0.079421 (0) + 0.060853 (1) - 0.003607 (0)\times(1)\right)}{ \exp\left(0.079421 (0) + 0.060853 (0) - 0.003607 (0)\times(0)\right)} \\
    &= \exp\left(0.060853 \right) \\
    &= 1.062743
\end{align*}
$$

:::

### Part (d)

The hazard ratio comparing postmenopausal patients at one year to premenopausal patients
at two years,
among patients who have no positive lymph nodes.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

Impossible.

Cox regression gives hazard ratios for a specific time $t$.
So, we could compare these groups at one year
or we can compare them at two years;
we can't compare one at one year to the other at two years.

:::

### Part (e)

The hazard ratio at time $t$ comparing postmenopausal to premenopausal patients,
among patients who have fifty positive lymph nodes.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

$\exp\left(0.079421   - 0.003607 (50)\right)$

$$
\begin{align*}
    \frac{\lambda_j(t)}{\lambda_i(t)} &= \frac{\lambda_0(t) \exp\left(0.079421 \texttt{meno}_j + 0.060853 \texttt{nodes}_j - 0.003607 \texttt{meno}_j\times\texttt{nodes}_j\right)}{\lambda_0(t) \exp\left(0.079421 \texttt{meno}_i + 0.060853 \texttt{nodes}_i - 0.003607 \texttt{meno}_i\times\texttt{nodes}_i\right)} \\
    &= \frac{\exp\left(0.079421 (1) + 0.060853 (50) - 0.003607 (1)\times(50)\right)}{\exp\left(0.079421 (0) + 0.060853 (50) - 0.003607 (0)\times(50)\right)} \\
    &= \exp\left(0.079421   - 0.003607 (50)\right) \\
\end{align*}
$$

:::

### Part (f)

The hazard ratio at time $t$ comparing patients with between 11 and 20 positive lymph nodes
to patients with between 1 and 10 positive lymph nodes,
among patients who are postmenopausal.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

Impossible.

If we wanted to estimate this, we would've had to create a new categorical variable
containing membership in these groups.

:::

### Part (g)

The probability that the test statistic corresponding to the coefficient
for `meno` would be at least as far from zero as it was in this data set,
assuming the true value of the coefficient was 0.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

0.592

This is the interpretation of the p-value.

:::

### Part (h)

The number of patients who were censored.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

387

The output tells us that the sample size was 686 and there were 299 events,
so $686-299=387$ patients were censored.

:::

### Part (i)

The median survival among premenopausal patients with one positive lymph node.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

Impossible.

If we had the hazard function, $h(t)$, we could find this value.
Since we only have hazard ratios, we can't compute survival probabilities.

:::

### Part (j)

The probability that the coefficient for `meno` is equal to 0.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

Impossible.

In frequentist statistics, parameters are fixed, not random,
so we don't compute probabilities like this.

:::
        


## Problem 2

(2 points)
Please provide a reasonable method to check the proportional hazards assumption in this analysis
and what results from that method would indicate that the assumption is met.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

You could conduct a Schoenfeld residual test.
High p-values would indicate that the assumption is met,
and low p-values would indicate that the assumption is not met.
Another way of saying this is that a non-significant result on the Schoenfeld residual test
would indicate that the assumption is met
and a non-significant result on the test would indicate that the assumption is not met.
It's not enough to just say ``check p-values''. You need to say
*what results from that method would indicate that the assumption is met*.

A complementary log-log-plot would not be reasonable for this analysis
because there are so many levels of the `nodes` variable.
However, you can still get a point for saying that parallel lines on the plot
would indicate that the assumption is met.

Looking at Kaplan-Meier curves would not be reasonable for this analysis
since `nodes` is effectively a continuous variable.
Even if there were no continuous variables, though, you couldn't check the PH assumptions
using a Kaplan-Meier curve.
The PH assumption implies that $S_1(t) = S_2(t)^c$.
How would you check this visually?
:::

## Problem 3

(2 points)
Do you think there is effect modification?
Justify your answer.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

No, because the p-value for the interaction term is very high.

You may have thought that, even if the p-value is high, there might be clinically meaningful
effect modification.
Let's consider an extreme case.
Consider part (e):
"The hazard ratio at time $t$ comparing postmenopausal to premenopausal patients,
among patients who have fifty positive lymph nodes."
This is $\exp\left(0.079421   - 0.003607 (50)\right) = 0.9039972$.
The hazard ratio at time $t$ comparing postmenopausal to premenopausal patients,
among patients who have zero positive lymph nodes,
is $\exp\left(0.079421 \right) = 1.08266$.
That's just not a huge difference in the effect of menopause for two wildly different
numbers of positive nodes.

:::
